 Published: November 3, 2026 By Lisa A. Tomaszewski, PhD  Marc B. Hahn, DO
 Federal student loan limits enacted under the rules of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act may unintentionally worsen the US physician shortage by making medical education less accessible, potentially shrinking the future physician workforce at a time when many communities already face significant delays in accessing care, according to Kansas City University President and Chief Executive Officer Mark B. Hahn, DO , in an opinion piece published in The Hill . 
 Physician’s Weekly (PW) spoke with Dr. Hahn to gain further insights into the potential impact of the student loan limits on the US physician shortage.
 PW: Why has it become more difficult for students to pursue a medical education, and what role is government policy playing? 
 Dr. Hahn: There have been some significant challenges—especially related to legislation that came out of the One Big Beautiful Bill —related to the funding of state Medicaid systems, the Medicare program, and health insurance plans related to the ACA [Affordable Care Act]. In addition, limitations have been placed on funding for various government agencies, such as the NIH and HRSSA [Health Resources and Services Administration]. Given the impact this legislation has had on capping student loans for medical students, dental students, and other healthcare professionals—and with funding being cut in multiple areas—we run the risk of negatively impacting medical education.
 You noted that medical students represent one of the strongest lending investments in higher education. Can you please elaborate on this? 
 Medical education is expensive, whether at a private institution such as ours, Kansas City University, or at a public institution. Annual tuition ranges from $40,000 to $80,000, and that’s just for the education component. Many medical students borrow for their living expenses. Unlike almost all other students, for medical students, their education is a full-time job. They’re not able to work a part-time job to earn money as they’re studying, so they end up borrowing. However, medical students, dental students, and other healthcare professionals pay back their loans. They borrow a quarter of a million dollars, but the default rate, as reported by the federal government, is less than 1.5%, and in many institutions, such as our own, it’s very close to that. So the default rate is extremely low, making medical students a good risk.
 How might the recent changes to federal student lending affect diversity within the future physician workforce? 
 One of the biggest risks we fear with the current federal student loan borrowing caps enacted on July 1st of this year involves students from diverse backgrounds, which basically means students from underrepresented minorities, from rural environments, military veterans, and other nontraditional students as well. These are the students who are less likely to be able to borrow money from the private sector. So, as the federal government caps lending through its various programs, this is forcing students into the private sector. This year, our institution engaged with nine private lenders and identified funding sources for all but one student. But in many cases, the students who can’t access private lending are those with lower credit scores. Perhaps they come from single-parent families, or perhaps they’re first-generation students; they’re not going to be able to borrow money at a competitive rate—or at the same rate as students from two-parent households or those with stronger credit scores.
 If these federal restrictions remain in place, what long-term consequences do you anticipate? 
 This is the first year that we’ve seen these federal caps on lending put in place. The main concern is that, as time goes by, more and more students will be required to borrow from the private sector.
 New lending restrictions and repayment rules also negatively affect other programs already in place, such as the Public Service Loan Forgiveness program. That program helps students in the medical profession write off federal loans after 10 years of public healthcare service in places such as community health centers, nonprofit and publicly funded hospitals, and Indian Health Service locations. Now we’ll have fewer medical students who can repay their loans by working in these underserved areas. This is just one of the unintended consequences.
 Another unintended consequence, as I said before, would be to discourage students who might not be creditworthy in the private lending industry from obtaining funds to attend medical, dental, and other healthcare professional programs. Again, these are students who may come from rural communities. They may come from historically underrepresented groups. They may be military veterans. They may be first-generation college students going into medical school. Among medical students, those are the folks most likely to return to those communities to care for them. If they’re taken out of the pool of medical students, we may see care in rural and urban underserved communities continue to decline because we won’t have physicians, dentists, and other healthcare providers returning to their communities.
 What steps can healthcare professionals take to address this issue? 
 Right now, the goal is increasing the cap the federal government has placed on professional student borrowers. That cap is currently at $200,000. As I mentioned, tuition alone for medical students costs from $40,000 to $80,000 a year, so the cap needs to be raised to adequately cover students’ expenses.
 There was recently proposed legislation by a bipartisan group of representatives—and the president said he might support it—in the House of Representatives: H.R. 2003. The legislation would cap all federal student loan interest rates at 2%. It would make borrowing much easier and, hopefully, make a big difference for medical students.
 Is there anything else you feel your physician peers should know regarding this issue? 
 There are a number of challenges these days in funding healthcare as well as funding basic science and clinical research. Now we’re also seeing challenges arising from lending mechanisms that are impacting students’ ability to attend school for medical, dental, and other healthcare professions. That’s a concern.
 There’s always reason for us to re-explore how we fund all of our activities—whether it’s financial services, research, or education—through tuition. We need to be concerned with doing the best job we can as physicians and administrators to ensure that the services we provide are cost-effective. At the same time, some of these challenges transcend reason and make it difficult for specific students in medical and business school to attend and succeed. We don’t want to make decisions on acceptance based on credit worthiness rather than merit. We want to be able to make the right decisions for everyone involved.
 Contributor 
 Marc B. Hahn, DO 
 Board-Certified Anesthesiologist

 October 22, 2026 Linda Girgis, MD, FAAFP  Linda Girgis, MD, FAAFP

 Monsters in Medicine
 14 Evil Doctors
 True Life Tales of Twisted Physicians
 When we think of evil doctors or monsters, we tend to imagine fictional characters like Frankenstein or Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. Although fictional horror can be chilling, real-life depravity proves far more terrifying. Among countless stories of true medical horror, these are my choices for the top 14 most evil doctors. 
 Read on—if you dare! 
 1. The “Angel of Death”
 Josef Mengele
 Josef Mengele, known as the “Angel of Death,” earned his medical degree in 1938 and later became Chief Camp Physician at Auschwitz. He performed brutal “selections,” deciding who would live or die, and conducted horrific experiments on prisoners, especially twins—injecting dyes into eyes, amputating limbs without anesthesia, and sewing twins together, causing fatal infections. After fleeing in 1945, he lived under aliases in South America until his death in 1979. DNA testing later confirmed his identity.
 2. The Poison Doctor
 Michael Swango
 From a young age, Michael Swango showed a morbid fascination with death. In medical school, several patients died under his care, earning him the nickname “Double-O.” Despite repeated violations, he graduated and began a surgical internship, where unexplained deaths and poisonings followed. After serving time for poisoning coworkers, he used aliases to keep working, killing patients in the US and Zimbabwe. Arrested in 1997, he is serving three life sentences.
 3. The Sterilization Nazi
 Carl Clauberg
 A gynecologist by training, Carl Clauberg joined the Nazi Party in 1938 and persuaded Heinrich Himmler to authorize sterilization experiments. At Auschwitz and Ravensbrück, he injected toxins into the uteruses of mostly Jewish women without anesthesia, causing agony, infection, and death, and ordered killings for autopsies. Arrested by Soviets after the war, he was sentenced to 25 years, released under repatriation, then rearrested in West Germany. He died in 1957 before trial.
 4. The Father of Lobotomy
 Walter Freeman
 American physician Walter Freeman, a proponent of psychosurgery, lacked surgical training but co-developed the first US prefrontal lobotomies. Seeking speed, he introduced the transorbital or “ice pick” lobotomy, inserting a metal rod behind the eye and severing brain connections. Many patients were left vegetative; about 490 died. Touring in his “lobotomobile,” he performed public demos, including on Rosemary Kennedy. After repeated deaths, his license was revoked. He died of cancer in 1972.
 5. The House Call Serial Killer
 Harold Shipman
 Harold Shipman, a general practitioner in England, was suspected after many of his patients died at home. An altered will naming him beneficiary led to an exhumation showing morphine overdose. Investigators found falsified records and drug hoarding. Convicted of 15 murders, he’s believed to have killed 236 patients. Shipman died by suicide in prison. 
 6. “Doctor Death”
 Jayant Patel
 Jayant Patel, an Indian-trained surgeon, began practicing in New York in 1984 but was soon fined and placed on probation for unsafe practices. New York revoked his license in 2001 after repeated patient harm. In Oregon, he faced multiple malpractice cases for unnecessary and fatal surgeries. Despite restrictions, he was hired in 2003 as director of surgery in Australia, where more deaths followed. Extradited in 2008, Patel was convicted, later appealed, and in 2013 pled guilty to fraud, receiving a suspended sentence.
 7. “Doctor Satan”
 Marcel Petiot
 Marcel Petiot, brilliant but unstable, earned a medical degree in 1921 and later became mayor of Villeneuve before repeated suspensions. Moving to Paris, he gained respect while secretly committing crimes. During WWII, he posed as a Resistance doctor helping Jews flee Nazi France but instead poisoned them, stole their valuables, and burned the bodies. Police found 30 corpses in his home in 1944. Petiot confessed to 60 murders, was convicted of 26, and was executed by guillotine in 1946.
 8. America’s First Serial Killer
 H. H. Holmes
 H. H. Holmes, often called America’s first serial killer, showed an early fascination with medicine and death. After medical school, he became a Chicago pharmacist and built his “Murder Castle,” equipped with trapdoors, gas chambers, and a cremation kiln. During the 1893 World’s Fair, he charmed victims, took over their finances, and killed them. He profited from insurance fraud and selling bodies. Convicted of murder, Holmes was executed; estimates of his victims exceed 200.
 9. The Kill-for-Inheritance Doctor
 John Bodkin Adams
 A general practioner in England, John Bodkin Adams gained a reputation for caring for elderly patients while showing a troubling interest in their wills and using risky drugs. In 1956, police investigated him for murdering patients to gain inheritances. Dozens of deaths appeared suspicious, but he was charged in only two cases, both involving large bequests. Acquitted of murder, he was convicted of forgery and falsifying records. He later resumed practice, and his case reshaped how England tried physicians.
 10. The Lambeth Poisoner
 Thomas Neill Cream
 Thomas Neill Cream practiced in Chicago, performing illegal abortions and poisoning patients, including Daniel Slott. Sentenced to life in prison, he was released in 1891 after his brother bribed officials. Moving to London, he poisoned prostitutes with strychnine and sent extortion letters blaming other doctors. Scotland Yard arrested and convicted him. At his 1892 execution, he allegedly began, “I am Jack the—,” sparking rumors he was Jack the Ripper, though he’d been imprisoned at the time.
 11. The Starvation Doctor
 Linda Burfield Hazzard
 Though not a medical doctor, Linda Hazzard gained a Washington license through a loophole and promoted fasting as a cure-all. At her sanitarium, patients endured extreme fasts, enemas, and violent “massages,” leading to at least 40 deaths. She blamed illness, but locals dubbed the site “Starvation Heights.” Convicted of manslaughter in 1912 after a wealthy patient died emaciated, she was later pardoned and moved to New Zealand, where she practiced until losing her license. She died in 1935.
 12. The Abortionist Killer
 Kermit Gosnell
 Kermit Gosnell, a Philadelphia physician, ran The Women’s Medical Society, which devolved into an illegal late-term abortion clinic. A 2010 raid revealed filthy conditions, untrained staff, and fetal remains stored in jars. One patient had died, and Gosnell admitted many abortions occurred past 24 weeks. Convicted of multiple murders and running a criminal enterprise, he received three life sentences without parole. A former assistant testified he’d seen more than 100 babies born alive whose necks Gosnell “snipped.”
 13. The Euthanasia Doctor
 Jack Kevorkian
 Jack Kevorkian, a US pathologist and euthanasia advocate nicknamed “Dr. Death,” built a $45 “suicide machine” that delivered lethal drugs. In 1990, he used it to help Alzheimer’s patient Janet Adkins end her life. Though charges were dropped, his license was revoked. He later assisted in more than 100 deaths. Convicted in 1999 of second-degree murder, he served eight years of a 25-year sentence and died in 2011 at age 83.
 14. The Mob Doctor
 Morris Bolber
 Morris “Louie the Rabbi” Bolber, a self-styled doctor, joined the 1930s “Philadelphia Poison Ring” led by cousins Herman and Paul Petrillo. Mixing folk magic with crime, Bolber supplied arsenic “potions” to kill victims insured by the gang. The Petrillos profited from fake policies and staged murders disguised as accidents. Between 1931 and 1939, 30 to 50 people died. Arrested in 1939, Bolber turned state’s evidence, and both Petrillos were sentenced to death.
 Final Reflections
 Real-life monsters appear in every walk of life. Do not assume that people in trusted roles are, in fact, trustworthy. Evil rarely announces itself; it hides behind pleasant manners and professional veneers. Keep your eyes open, think critically, and trust your instincts.
